sections.title: The island that says no
sections.intro_md: Most of India is crowded, connected and argued over. The Andaman and Nicobar Islands are where the country runs out of road. They sit in the Bay of Bengal closer to Myanmar, Thailand and Sumatra than to Chennai, a chain of forested islands on top of a drowned mountain range. One of them, North Sentinel, holds a people who have refused contact with the outside world for as long as anyone has records. Others hold a volcano, a jail that became a national shrine, India's only tri-service military command and a planned mega-port. Today is about how a remote archipelago carries so much of India's history, biology and future.

spotlights.name: North Sentinel Island

where.label: North Sentinel, about 50 km west of Sri Vijaya Puram

spotlights.spot_it: A small, flat, forest-covered island ringed by a wide white reef, with no jetty, no road and no smoke you can photograph.
spotlights.story_md: North Sentinel is about **60 square km** of forest, part of India, and almost nobody has ever set foot on it. The Sentinelese who live there have made it clear for at least 150 years, mostly with arrows, that they want to be left alone. The 2011 census could only count **15** of them from a distance; estimates run from about 50 to 200. Three days after the 2004 earthquake, a government helicopter flew over to check if they had survived. Islanders came out on the beach and shot arrows and threw spears and stones at it. In March 2025 an American YouTuber landed illegally and left a can of Diet Coke and a coconut on the shore. He was arrested within days.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is one of the last places on Earth where a society lives entirely on its own terms, and India's law is built to keep it that way.
spotlights.memory_hook: The world's most private island answered a rescue helicopter with arrows.

spotlights.name: An archipelago the length of a country

where.label: From Landfall Island to Indira Point

spotlights.spot_it: A long broken chain of green islands, 800 km north to south, in water so clear the reefs show from orbit.
spotlights.story_md: Stand on the map's north tip, Landfall Island, and the southern tip, Indira Point, is about **800 km** away, roughly Delhi to Ahmedabad. In between lie **836 islands and islets**, of which only about **31** are permanently lived on. They are the tops of a drowned mountain chain, the same one that rises as the Arakan Yoma in Myanmar and continues south as the islands off Sumatra. Port Blair is about 1,190 km from Chennai, but Indonesia is only about 165 km from Indira Point and Myanmar's Coco Islands sit just off the northern tip. India's mainland is farther from these islands than three foreign countries are.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It explains everything here: the isolation, the strategy, the earthquakes and the endemic animals.
spotlights.memory_hook: Closer to Sumatra than to Chennai.

sections.title: The islands in numbers
sections.intro_md: The territory is a union territory run from Delhi through a Lieutenant Governor, with one Lok Sabha seat and three districts: North and Middle Andaman, South Andaman, and Nicobar. Its 836 islands and islets cover 8,249 square km, about four-fifths the size of Tripura, yet they stretch across 800 km of sea. About 86% of the land is forest, one of the highest shares in India, and only about 6% can be farmed. The 2011 census counted 3,80,581 people, so density is low, about 46 per square km against India's 382. The capital holds about a third of everyone.

spotlights.name: Sri Vijaya Puram (Port Blair)
spotlights.spot_it: A hilly harbour town of tin roofs and concrete, a clock tower at Aberdeen Bazaar, ferries and naval ships in the bay.
spotlights.story_md: The capital was named in 1789 after **Archibald Blair**, the naval surveyor who first charted its harbour for the East India Company. In September 2024 the Union Home Minister announced the new name, **Sri Vijaya Puram**, to shed the colonial label. The name points back about 1,000 years: the Chola king Rajendra I is believed to have used the islands as a base for his 1025 CE raid on the Srivijaya empire in Sumatra. About a third of the territory's people live in and around the town. Almost everything, from cement to onions, arrives at Haddo Wharf by ship.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Every journey to the islands starts here, and so does every argument about what they should be called.
spotlights.memory_hook: Named for a British surveyor, renamed for a Chola raid.

spotlights.name: The Ten Degree Channel

where.label: Between Little Andaman and Car Nicobar

spotlights.spot_it: A 150 km gap of open, deep water along the 10th parallel with the Andamans to the north and the Nicobars to the south.
spotlights.story_md: The two halves of the territory are not one archipelago with one story. The **Ten Degree Channel**, about **150 km** wide, separates them, and the split runs through everything. The Andaman group is bigger (6,408 square km) and was peopled by Negrito-looking hunter-gatherers whose ancestors arrived tens of thousands of years ago. The Nicobar group (1,841 square km) was settled far later by Austroasiatic-speaking people related to the mainland Southeast Asian language family that includes Khmer. Each half even has its own wildlife: the hornbill of Narcondam and the megapode of the Nicobars never cross the channel.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It turns one territory into two different worlds.
spotlights.memory_hook: Ten degrees north, two different peoples.

spotlights.name: Mount Harriet, now Mount Manipur, on the 20 rupee note

where.label: Mount Manipur National Park, South Andaman

spotlights.spot_it: A forested hill above Port Blair with a viewpoint over green islands, a bay and a lighthouse: the view on the old 20 rupee note.
spotlights.story_md: Pull out a pre-2019 **20 rupee note** and turn it over: the coconut palms and sea are the view from Mount Harriet, across the water from Port Blair. The hill was named after **Harriet Tytler**, wife of a convict settlement superintendent in the 1860s. In 2021 its national park was renamed **Mount Manipur**, honouring the Manipuri leaders exiled here after the 1891 Anglo-Manipur war. At about 383 m it is one of the highest points in the south, and the forest trail is one of the best places to see the island's endemic birds and butterflies.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Millions of Indians carried an Andaman view in their wallets without knowing it.
spotlights.memory_hook: Your old 20 rupee note was a postcard from Port Blair.

sections.title: Volcanoes, mud and caves
sections.intro_md: The islands are the crest of an undersea mountain range pushed up where the Indian plate grinds under the Burma plate. That collision is still going, and you can see it. Barren Island erupts, Narcondam is a dormant cone, Baratang's mud volcanoes burp up cold sediment from deep below, and limestone formed on the seabed now stands in hills and caves. Rain falls in two monsoons, and dense evergreen forest covers almost everything. The same plate boundary produced the 2004 earthquake, which lifted parts of the north by a metre or more and dropped the south by several.

spotlights.name: Barren Island volcano

where.label: Barren Island, 138 km north-east of Port Blair

spotlights.spot_it: A dark cone rising inside a broken ring of green hills, alone in the sea, often with a plume of ash.
spotlights.story_md: Barren Island is the only confirmed active volcano in South Asia. It is small, about **8.3 square km**, and rises to about 353 m, but it sits above the line where the Indian plate dives under the Burma plate. Eruptions were recorded in 1787, then it went quiet for about 150 years until **1991**, when it erupted for six months. Since January 2022 it has been erupting on and off. In 2025 it erupted on **13 and 20 September**, and on 2 October an ash plume rose to about 3,000 m. No people live there. Its only residents are feral goats, descendants of animals left by sailors in 1891.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is the visible proof that the islands sit on a live plate boundary.
spotlights.memory_hook: India's only live volcano is ruled by goats.

spotlights.name: Narcondam Island
spotlights.spot_it: A steep, forest-clad volcanic cone standing alone in the Andaman Sea, far east of the main chain.
spotlights.story_md: Barren Island's quieter sibling lies about 120 km to its north. Narcondam is a dormant volcano of **6.8 square km**, covered in forest, with a small police outpost set up in 1969 and nothing else. It matters because of one bird. The **Narcondam hornbill** lives here and nowhere else, so the whole species fits on an island you can walk across in a morning. In 2012 India's environment ministry turned down a Coast Guard plan for a radar station on the island because of the hornbill, a rare case of a bird beating a security project.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It shows how one small island can hold an entire species.
spotlights.memory_hook: An island the size of a town, holding a whole species.

spotlights.name: The Baratang mud volcano
spotlights.spot_it: A low grey mound in the forest with bubbling pools of cold mud, ringed by a wooden walkway.
spotlights.story_md: Baratang has India's best known **mud volcanoes**. They are not hot: gas from deep underground pushes cold, salty mud up to the surface, where it builds small cones. On **2 October 2025**, after about 20 years of only minor activity, the main vent erupted with a loud bang. It threw up a mound 3 to 4 m high, spread mud over more than 1,000 square metres and wrecked the visitor walkway. The Geological Survey of India sampled the mud and dated the material to the **Oligocene, about 23 million years ago**. The Andamans have at least 11 mud volcanoes in all.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is a window into rock layers 23 million years old.
spotlights.memory_hook: A volcano that erupts cold mud older than the Himalayas' peaks.

spotlights.name: Baratang limestone caves
spotlights.spot_it: Narrow passages of pale, glittering rock with stalactites, reached by a speedboat ride through mangrove tunnels.
spotlights.story_md: The caves are a lesson in how the islands were built. The limestone formed from shells and coral on an ancient seabed, was pushed up by the same plate collision that drives Barren Island, and then dissolved slowly by rainwater into passages and dripping stalactites. Getting there is half the point: from the Baratang jetty you take a boat along a creek where the mangroves close overhead, then walk about 1.5 km through village fields. Torchlight brings out mineral sparkles in the rock. The caves are a stop on the road north, which itself runs through the Jarawa reserve.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is the easiest way for a visitor to see the islands' geology up close.
spotlights.memory_hook: A seabed lifted into the sky, then hollowed by rain.

spotlights.name: Mangrove creeks
spotlights.spot_it: Trees standing in seawater on arched stilt roots, forming green tunnels along tidal creeks.
spotlights.story_md: Mangroves line hundreds of kilometres of Andaman creeks. Their stilt and breathing roots let them live in salty, airless mud, and they trap sediment, nurse young fish and crabs, and blunt storm waves. In 2004 they showed their value the hard way: the tsunami did some of its worst damage where mangroves had been cleared for farms and settlements. Then the earthquake itself changed the map. Parts of the islands sank by about a metre, drowning some mangrove belts, while others rose and left mangroves high and dry. Today the creek rides at Baratang and Havelock are among the islands' most popular trips.
spotlights.why_it_matters: They are the coast's shock absorber, and the 2004 quake rearranged them overnight.
spotlights.memory_hook: Trees on stilts that hold the coast together.

sections.title: Reefs, sea cows and giants
sections.intro_md: The islands give India nearly a third of its sea territory and some of its richest reefs. The water is clear because there are no big rivers dumping silt, and the reefs fringe almost every coast. The sea also holds the territory's state animal, the dugong, the largest turtle on Earth, the largest reptile and the largest land crab. Most of them are rare, and several are tied directly to the fight over Great Nicobar's future. Reefs have been bleached by warm-water years and reshaped by the 2004 quake, but they remain the reason most visitors come.

spotlights.name: Coral reefs and Mahatma Gandhi Marine National Park

where.label: Wandoor and Jolly Buoy, South Andaman

spotlights.spot_it: Glass-clear water over branching and brain corals, with snorkellers floating above, and white beaches on uninhabited islets.
spotlights.story_md: The islands have some of India's largest and healthiest coral reefs, fringing almost every coast. **Mahatma Gandhi Marine National Park** at Wandoor, south-west of Port Blair, protects a cluster of 15 islands and their reefs; Jolly Buoy and Red Skin are the ones visitors can reach, and plastic bottles are banned on the boats. Havelock's Elephant Beach is the busiest snorkelling spot. The reefs are fragile. Warm-water events have bleached them repeatedly, and in 2004 the earthquake lifted some reefs clean out of the water in the north, killing them, while others in the south sank deeper.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Reefs are the reason most tourists come, and the first thing a warming sea damages.
spotlights.memory_hook: A garden you can only see with your face in the water.

spotlights.name: Dugong, the state animal

where.label: Seagrass beds off Ritchie's Archipelago and Little Andaman

spotlights.spot_it: A grey, rounded sea mammal with a whale-like tail and a down-turned snout, grazing on seagrass.
spotlights.story_md: The dugong is a relative of the elephant that went back to the sea. It eats almost nothing but seagrass, tens of kilograms a day, ploughing furrows along the bottom like a slow cow. That is why sailors called it the sea cow, and why some think dugongs seen from a distance fed old stories of mermaids. It is the territory's **state animal**, yet it is rare: India's whole population is thought to be a few hundred animals spread over the Gulf of Mannar, Palk Bay, the Gulf of Kutch and these islands. The Onge and other islanders once hunted it; today it is fully protected.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is a flagship for the seagrass meadows that feed fish and hold sand in place.
spotlights.memory_hook: The mermaid is a vegetarian cousin of the elephant.

spotlights.name: Leatherback turtles of Great Nicobar
spotlights.spot_it: A huge dark turtle with a soft, ridged, leathery back instead of a hard shell, hauling itself up a beach at night.
spotlights.story_md: The leatherback is the **largest turtle alive**: adults can pass 2 m and weigh more than 500 kg. It dives deeper than 1,000 m to hunt jellyfish and crosses whole oceans. Some of its most important nesting beaches in the Indian Ocean are on Great Nicobar and Little Andaman, with **Galathea Bay** the best known. The 2004 tsunami washed away many nesting beaches, and the turtles came back within a few seasons. Now Galathea Bay is the planned site of a giant container port, which is why this one animal sits at the centre of India's fiercest environmental court fight.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Its beach is where India's biggest island project is meant to be built.
spotlights.memory_hook: A turtle the weight of a small car nests on the site of a planned mega-port.

spotlights.name: Saltwater crocodile

where.label: Mangrove creeks of Middle and North Andaman

spotlights.spot_it: A massive grey-brown crocodile with a broad snout, basking on a mudbank or cruising a creek with only eyes and nostrils showing.
spotlights.story_md: The saltwater crocodile is the largest living reptile, with big males over 6 m, and it is at home in both creeks and the open sea. The Andamans hold one of India's three main populations, with the Sundarbans and Bhitarkanika in Odisha. Crocodiles move between islands by sea, which is why some popular beaches carry warning signs and why swimming in creek mouths at dusk is a bad idea. Numbers recovered after hunting was banned under the Wildlife Protection Act of 1972, and conflict with people has risen as settlements and tourism spread along the coast.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is the islands' top predator and a real safety issue on some beaches.
spotlights.memory_hook: The biggest reptile on Earth commutes between islands by sea.

spotlights.name: Coconut crab (robber crab)
spotlights.spot_it: A crab as big as a cat, blue, purple or orange, climbing a palm trunk at night or cracking a coconut with its claws.
spotlights.story_md: The coconut crab is the **largest land-living arthropod** in the world: it can weigh about 4 kg and span almost a metre leg to leg. Young ones live in borrowed snail shells like hermit crabs, then outgrow them and harden their own armour. Adults cannot swim and would drown in the sea where they were born. Their claws can crush a coconut husk, and they are known to steal shiny objects, which is where the name robber crab comes from. The Nicobars and some Andaman islets hold India's only populations, and they are protected under Schedule I of the Wildlife Protection Act.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is a giant that survives only on islands with few people.
spotlights.memory_hook: A crab that climbs trees, cracks coconuts and steals spoons.

sections.title: Animals found nowhere else
sections.intro_md: Islands make new species. Cut off from the mainland for long periods, animals here drifted into forms of their own, and the territory has an unusually high share of endemics: of about 270 bird species, about 90 are endemic species or subspecies, and of about 55 mammals, 32 are endemic. Over 8,300 animal species are recorded, 1,117 of them endemic. The Ten Degree Channel splits the fauna too: the Andamans and Nicobars each have their own specialities. Add the animals people brought, from deer on Ross Island to elephants on Interview Island, and you get an odd, fragile mix.

spotlights.name: Narcondam hornbill
spotlights.spot_it: A black hornbill with a pale yellowish bill and casque; males have a rufous head and neck, females are all black.
spotlights.story_md: Every Narcondam hornbill alive lives on one 6.8 square km island, the smallest range of any Asian hornbill. Estimates have risen with better surveys: about 200 birds in 1905, around 430 to 500 in 2002, and a 2019 to 2020 count that the IUCN converted to **300 to 650 mature birds**. Hunting by the police outpost staff once took 25 to 40 birds a year until an awareness campaign stopped it. Feral goats that ate the seedlings of its food trees have been removed. One cyclone or disease could still wipe it out, which is why it is listed as endangered.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is a whole species with no backup population.
spotlights.memory_hook: One island, one hornbill, no spare copies.

spotlights.name: Nicobar megapode
spotlights.spot_it: A plain brown, hen-sized bird with big feet scratching on the forest edge near a beach, next to a large mound of sand and leaves.
spotlights.story_md: The megapode does not sit on its eggs. Pairs pile up mounds of sand, leaves and twigs, sometimes more than **10 cubic metres**, and bury their eggs inside. Bacteria rotting the leaves produce the heat, and the eggs incubate for **70 to 80 days**. The chick digs itself out fully feathered and can fly as soon as its feathers dry; it never meets its parents. Because the mounds sit just behind the beach, the 2004 tsunami was a disaster for the bird: the population fell by an estimated **two-thirds to three-quarters**.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is a coastal specialist with no fallback when the coast changes.
spotlights.memory_hook: A bird that uses compost as a mother.

spotlights.name: Nicobar pigeon
spotlights.spot_it: A heavy pigeon with long metallic green and copper neck hackles and a short white tail.
spotlights.story_md: This is the most glamorous pigeon on Earth, and the islands gave it its name. Its long iridescent neck feathers flash green, blue and bronze. It feeds on the ground and island-hops in flocks, roosting on small islets where predators are few. DNA studies show it is the **closest living relative of the extinct dodo** of Mauritius, part of a group of island pigeons spread across the Indian Ocean and the Pacific. It still lives in the Nicobars and on Narcondam, though hunting and the loss of small islet forests have cut its numbers.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It links these islands to the most famous extinction story in history.
spotlights.memory_hook: The dodo's nearest living cousin is a shiny Nicobar pigeon.

spotlights.name: Andaman wood pigeon, the state bird
spotlights.spot_it: A large dark grey pigeon with a pale whitish head, high in the canopy of tall evergreen forest.
spotlights.story_md: The **state bird** is not a showy one. The Andaman wood pigeon is found only in the Andaman and Nicobar Islands, living in the canopy of old evergreen forest and eating fruits. It is rated near threatened because it depends on big trees, and big trees were the islands' main export for more than a century. That makes it a good symbol: of about **270 bird species** recorded in the territory, roughly **90** are endemic species or subspecies, the highest share of anywhere in India. Mount Manipur's forest trail is the best place to look for it.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It stands for the forest-dependent birds that exist nowhere else.
spotlights.memory_hook: A grey pigeon with a white head: the badge of 90 endemic birds.

spotlights.name: Andaman padauk, the state tree
spotlights.spot_it: A tall tree with a buttressed trunk, yellow flowers and flat round winged pods; its timber is deep red.
spotlights.story_md: Andaman padauk produces one of the world's finest red timbers, so heavy and stable that it was used for furniture, carving and the panelling of grand rooms in Britain. The tree is endemic to the islands, and for more than a century it was the forest's most valuable export. The British built the **Chatham Saw Mill** in 1883 largely to process timber like it. Large-scale logging ended after a 2002 Supreme Court order restricted felling, and today the islands' forest cover is about **86%** of their land, one of the highest shares in India.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is the tree that drove the islands' colonial economy.
spotlights.memory_hook: Red wood that panelled British rooms grew only here.

spotlights.name: Andaman day gecko
spotlights.spot_it: A bright lime-green gecko with red speckles on its back, out in daylight on coconut trunks and house walls.
spotlights.story_md: Most geckos come out at night and are dull brown. The Andaman day gecko breaks both rules: it is vivid green, hunts in daylight, and laps nectar and fruit as well as eating insects. Its nearest relatives are the day geckos of Madagascar and the Mascarene islands, thousands of kilometres away across the Indian Ocean, which makes its presence here a small puzzle of how lizards spread across oceans. It is found only in the Andaman and Nicobar Islands and is often seen on coconut palms in villages, where it seems to like the shelter of leaf bases.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is one of the easiest endemic animals a visitor can see.
spotlights.memory_hook: A Madagascar-green lizard, stranded in the Andamans.

spotlights.name: Rajan, the swimming elephant
spotlights.spot_it: Elephants are not native to the islands; Rajan was the last famous one, filmed swimming in open sea over the reefs.
spotlights.story_md: There are no wild elephants in the Andamans. People brought them from the mainland as timber workers, and they had to learn to **swim logs out to barges** offshore. Rajan arrived in the 1970s. When logging was curbed in the early 2000s most elephants went back to the mainland, but he stayed on Havelock, where a resort bought him in 2007 and he became a celebrity, swimming with divers and appearing in Tarsem Singh's film *The Fall* (2006). He retired in 2014 and died in 2016 at about 66. Feral descendants of other working elephants still live wild on Interview Island.
spotlights.why_it_matters: He is the gentle face of the islands' logging past.
spotlights.memory_hook: The elephant that went scuba diving.

sections.title: The first peoples
sections.intro_md: Before any settler, two very different groups lived here. In the Andamans: the Great Andamanese, Jarawa, Onge and Sentinelese, hunter-gatherers whose ancestors are thought to have reached the islands tens of thousands of years ago, and who stayed largely cut off until the 1800s. In the Nicobars: the Nicobarese, gardeners and traders who speak an Austroasiatic language, and the Shompen of Great Nicobar's forests. Contact went worst for the Great Andamanese. Today five of these groups are classed as Particularly Vulnerable Tribal Groups, and India's policy for the most isolated is to protect them by leaving them alone.

spotlights.name: The Great Andamanese
spotlights.when: Ten tribes in 1789; about 59 people in 2020
spotlights.spot_it: Old photographs of people with shaved heads and white clay patterns on skin, outrigger canoes, and today a small village on Strait Island.
spotlights.story_md: When the British arrived in 1789 the main Andaman islands were home to **ten Great Andamanese tribes**, each with its own language, perhaps 2,000 to 6,600 people in all. Contact was catastrophic. Measles, syphilis, influenza and alcohol killed far more than guns did. The count fell to **625 by 1901** and to just **19 in 1961**. Survivors were moved to Bluff Island in 1949 and then to Strait Island in 1969, where their numbers have slowly recovered, to 59 in 2020. The ten languages have merged into one mixed Great Andamanese, and most people now speak Hindi.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is one of the clearest records of what colonial contact did to isolated peoples.
spotlights.memory_hook: Ten tribes, then nineteen people.

spotlights.name: Boa Sr, the last speaker of Bo
spotlights.spot_it: An elderly Great Andamanese woman, laughing in a pink blouse, remembered from linguists' recordings of songs nobody else could understand.
spotlights.story_md: For the last 30 to 40 years of her life, Boa Sr had **no one left to talk to** in her own language. She was the last fluent speaker of Bo, one of the ten Great Andamanese languages. The linguist **Anvita Abbi** of Jawaharlal Nehru University recorded her words and songs. Boa had survived the 2004 tsunami by climbing a tree. She died in Port Blair on **26 January 2010**, at about 85, and Bo died with her. Languages of the Andamans are thought to belong to lineages tens of thousands of years old, so her death closed a door that cannot be reopened.
spotlights.why_it_matters: One death ended a language that may have been spoken here for tens of thousands of years.
spotlights.memory_hook: She sang to birds because no person spoke her language.

spotlights.name: The Jarawa and the Andaman Trunk Road

where.label: Jarawa Tribal Reserve, South and Middle Andaman

spotlights.spot_it: A forest highway with buses waiting in a convoy at a checkpost, with signs banning stops, photos and gifts.
spotlights.story_md: The Jarawa are hunter-gatherers of the western forests of South and Middle Andaman, about **380** people in the 2011 census. For a century they fought off outsiders. In the 1970s the **Andaman Trunk Road** was cut straight through their land, and from 1997-98 Jarawa began walking out of the forest on their own. Measles followed in 1999 and 2006. In 2012 a video of Jarawa women being told to dance for tourists in exchange for food caused an outcry. Today vehicles cross the reserve only in timed convoys, and stopping, photographing or feeding Jarawa is a crime.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is a live test of whether a road and a free people can share the same forest.
spotlights.memory_hook: A national highway runs through a hunter-gatherer homeland.

spotlights.name: The Onge of Little Andaman
spotlights.spot_it: Two small settlements on Little Andaman, people who once hunted turtle and dugong from dugout canoes.
spotlights.story_md: The Onge numbered **672 in 1901** and **101 in 2011**, now living in two reserve camps at Dugong Creek and South Bay on Little Andaman. On 26 December 2004 the ground shook hard, and Onge elders remembered a story handed down for generations: a big shaking is followed by a wall of water. They led everyone up into the hills. **Almost all Onge survived** a tsunami that killed thousands of settlers on the same island. In 2008 tragedy came from the sea instead: eight Onge men died after drinking a liquid, probably methanol, from a container that washed ashore.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Their oral history worked better than any warning system in 2004.
spotlights.memory_hook: An old story saved a whole people.

spotlights.name: The Shompen of Great Nicobar
spotlights.spot_it: Forest people of Great Nicobar's interior, photographed only a handful of times, here in 1886.
spotlights.story_md: The Shompen live deep in the rainforest of Great Nicobar, about **229** people in the 2011 census, perhaps 200 to 300 in total, most of them never contacted. They hunt, gather, keep pigs and grow yams and pandanus, moving between small camps of communal huts. Their language is barely documented and may be unrelated to Nicobarese. In 2024, **39 genocide scholars** wrote to India's President warning that the Great Nicobar mega-project, with its port, airport and new city, could be a death sentence for the Shompen, because they have little immunity to outside diseases.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Their future is the hardest question the Great Nicobar project has to answer.
spotlights.memory_hook: The people at the centre of a mega-port they have never heard of.

spotlights.name: The Nicobarese
spotlights.spot_it: Islanders in canoes and coconut groves, dancing in a ring with leaf headdresses at the Ossuary feast or on Island Tourism Festival stages.
spotlights.story_md: The Nicobarese, about **28,900** people in 2011, are the largest tribal community in the territory. They call themselves **Holchu**, meaning friend. Their language belongs to the Austroasiatic family, the same as Khmer and Mon, which points to roots in mainland Southeast Asia. Around 95% are Christian, mostly through the work of **John Richardson**, a Nicobarese teacher and later bishop who translated the New Testament. Land and coconut groves belong to the family group, not to individuals, and village life is run by elected captains and councils. Women choose their husbands.
spotlights.why_it_matters: They show a tribal society that has absorbed a world religion without giving up its land system.
spotlights.memory_hook: Holchu means friend, and it is what they call themselves.

sections.title: Chola fleets, Danes and the penal colony
sections.intro_md: Sailors from India, China and the Arab world knew the islands for centuries, mostly as a place to avoid: Marco Polo repeated stories of dog-headed cannibals. The first firm Indian record is Chola. Europeans came in the 1700s, Danes in the Nicobars and the British in the Andamans in 1789, but disease drove them out. The real turning point was 1857. After the great uprising, the British needed somewhere far away to send thousands of rebels, and in March 1858 they founded a penal settlement at Port Blair. For the next 80 years, the islands were a prison.

spotlights.name: Rajendra Chola's island base
spotlights.spot_it: A Tamil king's war fleet, recorded in a temple inscription at Thanjavur that names the islands Ma-Nakkavaram.
spotlights.story_md: Around **1025 CE** the Chola emperor **Rajendra I** sent a fleet across the Bay of Bengal to strike the Srivijaya empire in Sumatra, which controlled the Strait of Malacca. The islands lay on the route. A Thanjavur inscription of about **1050 CE** lists them as **Ma-Nakkavaram**, often glossed as land of the naked, and that word is the likely root of the name Nicobar. Marco Polo later wrote of Necuveran. In 2024 the Indian government cited this voyage when it renamed Port Blair as Sri Vijaya Puram, after the city of victory over Srivijaya.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It gives the islands their oldest written name and India's main historical claim to them.
spotlights.memory_hook: Nicobar comes from a Tamil inscription about naked islanders.

spotlights.name: The Danish Nicobars
spotlights.spot_it: Old maps naming the islands Frederiksøerne, and a Danish warship anchored off a palm-lined shore.
spotlights.story_md: For more than a century the Nicobars were a **Danish colony**. The Danish East India Company claimed them in 1755-56 and named them **Frederiksøerne**, Frederick's Islands. Moravian missionaries arrived in 1768, and the settlers kept dying of malaria; the colony was abandoned and reoccupied several times. An Austrian adventurer, William Bolts, even tried to plant an Austrian colony from 1778 to 1783. The corvette Galathea came in 1846 to try again, which is why Great Nicobar has a **Galathea Bay**. Denmark finally sold its rights to Britain on **16 October 1868**.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Few Indians know that part of India was once Danish.
spotlights.memory_hook: Galathea Bay is named after a Danish warship.

spotlights.name: The Battle of Aberdeen
spotlights.spot_it: A memorial plaque at Aberdeen jetty in the capital, the only monument in India to a battle fought with bows against rifles.
spotlights.story_md: In 1858 the British reopened a penal colony on the islands, using convicts from the 1857 uprising to clear the forest. The Great Andamanese saw their land being cut down and fought back. On **17 May 1859**, hundreds of Andamanese attacked the settlement at Aberdeen with bows and arrows. The British were ready. An escaped convict named **Dudhnath Tewari**, who had lived with the Andamanese for over a year and married into the community, slipped back and warned them. Rifles won. Tewari was pardoned. The Andamanese lost the battle and, within a few decades, most of their people.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It was the last stand of the Great Andamanese against colonisation.
spotlights.memory_hook: Bows against rifles, betrayed by a runaway convict.

spotlights.name: The assassination of Lord Mayo

where.label: Hope Town jetty, Sri Vijaya Puram

spotlights.spot_it: A Victorian engraving of a viceroy stabbed on a jetty at dusk, and a photograph of his killer in chains.
spotlights.story_md: On **8 February 1872** the Viceroy of India, **Lord Mayo**, came to inspect the convict settlement. As he walked back to his boat at dusk, a convict named **Sher Ali Afridi** sprang out and stabbed him in the back. Mayo died within minutes. Sher Ali, a Pashtun who had served in the colonial forces, was serving a life term for killing a relative and had sworn revenge on the British for what he saw as an unjust sentence. He was hanged on Viper Island on 11 March 1872. He remains the only person to have killed a sitting Viceroy of India.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is the only time a Viceroy of India was assassinated.
spotlights.memory_hook: The most powerful man in India, killed by a prisoner at a jetty.

spotlights.name: Viper Island
spotlights.spot_it: A small wooded island in the harbour with brick ruins and a gallows on its summit.
spotlights.story_md: Before the Cellular Jail there was Viper. The island is named after the **Viper**, the ship of Archibald Blair, whose wreck is said to lie nearby. The British built a jail here in 1864-67 for the hardest cases, and convicts knew it as the Viper chain gang jail because prisoners worked in fetters. Its gallows still stand on the hilltop, and Lord Mayo's assassin was hanged there in 1872. Once the Cellular Jail opened in 1906, Viper was abandoned. Today the jail has collapsed to its plinth, and a harbour cruise from the capital stops at the island.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is the forgotten first chapter of Kala Pani.
spotlights.memory_hook: The gallows came before the cells.

spotlights.name: Ross Island (Netaji Subhas Chandra Bose Dweep)
spotlights.spot_it: Red brick ruins of churches, clubs and bungalows gripped by giant tree roots, with deer and peacocks walking among them.
spotlights.story_md: For 80 years the tiny island at the mouth of the harbour was the British capital of the settlement. The officers lived here in comfort with a church, a bakery, a ballroom and a swimming pool while convicts toiled across the water; some called it the Paris of the East. The first convicts landed in **March 1858**. An earthquake in **1941** damaged the buildings and the Japanese took the island in 1942 and dug bunkers. The ruins were left to the jungle. In December 2018 it was renamed **Netaji Subhas Chandra Bose Dweep**.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is the best place to see how the colonial settlement actually lived.
spotlights.memory_hook: A ballroom eaten by a tree.

spotlights.name: Maurice Vidal Portman
spotlights.when: In charge of the Andamanese 1879 to 1901
spotlights.spot_it: A Victorian officer with a camera, whose glass plates are the main photographs we have of the Andamanese before 1900.
spotlights.story_md: Portman was the British officer in charge of relations with the Andamanese for about two decades, and an obsessive photographer and recorder of their languages. He is also the man who, in **1880**, led a party onto North Sentinel Island and **carried off six people**, an elderly couple and four children. The two adults soon died of illness in Port Blair, and the children were returned to the island with gifts. Researchers think this episode, and the diseases it may have carried, could be one reason the Sentinelese have been so fiercely hostile ever since.
spotlights.why_it_matters: His archive is invaluable, and his raid may explain the Sentinelese's hostility.
spotlights.memory_hook: The man who photographed a people also kidnapped their neighbours.

sections.title: Kala Pani
sections.intro_md: For Indians, the Andamans meant one thing for almost a century: transportation for life across the black water. Convicts came from all over British India, ordinary criminals and political prisoners alike, and most never went back. From the 1900s the islands became the place to bury the most dangerous revolutionaries, from Bengal's bomb-makers to the Ghadar rebels of Punjab, inside a jail designed to break them through isolation and labour. Today the Cellular Jail is a National Memorial, and visiting it has become a kind of national pilgrimage.

spotlights.name: Cellular Jail
spotlights.spot_it: A three-storey brick prison with long wings radiating from a central watch tower, like the spokes of a wheel.
spotlights.story_md: Kala Pani, black water, was what Indians called a sentence to the islands: crossing the sea was thought to cost a person their caste, and few came back. The **Cellular Jail** was built from 1896 to 1906 for **₹5,17,352**. It had seven wings and **696 cells**, all for solitary confinement. The wings were arranged so that each row of cells faced the back of the next wing, so no prisoner could see or signal another. Prisoners were yoked to oil mills and made to grind coconut oil to a daily quota. Only three wings and the tower survive.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is the national symbol of what the freedom struggle cost.
spotlights.memory_hook: Every cell door faced a blank wall.

spotlights.name: V. D. Savarkar in the Cellular Jail
spotlights.spot_it: A narrow cell on an upper floor with a portrait and garlands, the most visited cell in the jail.
spotlights.story_md: **Vinayak Damodar Savarkar** arrived in July 1911 to serve two life terms, 50 years, for revolutionary activity. His older brother **Ganesh** was already a prisoner in the same jail. Savarkar filed mercy petitions in 1911, 1913, 1917 and 1920; supporters see them as tactics to get out and keep working, critics as surrender, and the debate is still politically hot. He was moved to the mainland in May 1921. Today his cell is kept like a shrine, and the island's airport carries his name.
spotlights.why_it_matters: He is the jail's most famous and most argued-over prisoner.
spotlights.memory_hook: Two brothers, one jail, ten years.

spotlights.name: The 1933 hunger strike
spotlights.spot_it: No photograph survives of the strike itself; the memorial lists the names of the men who died.
spotlights.story_md: In 1933 political prisoners in the Cellular Jail went on hunger strike against their treatment: bad food, no reading, harsh punishments. The jail authorities tried to break it by **force-feeding** through tubes. Three prisoners died after force-feeding: **Mahavir Singh**, a comrade of Bhagat Singh, **Mohan Kishore Namadas** and **Mohit Moitra**. The deaths made news on the mainland. After pressure from Mahatma Gandhi, Rabindranath Tagore and others, the government began sending political prisoners home in **1937-38**, and the jail was emptied of them by 1939.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is the moment Kala Pani's cruelty became impossible to hide.
spotlights.memory_hook: Three men killed by being fed.

sections.title: Japan, Bose and new names
sections.intro_md: The Second World War brought the only foreign occupation of Indian soil in that war. Japan took the islands in March 1942 and, at the end of 1943, handed nominal control to Subhas Chandra Bose's Azad Hind government. The occupation was brutal, and its memory is mixed: the first raising of the tricolour on liberated soil, alongside torture and massacres. Since 2018 the Indian government has leaned heavily on the Bose story, renaming islands and planning a Netaji memorial on Ross Island.

spotlights.name: Japanese bunkers

where.label: Ross Island, Chatham and Corbyn's Cove

spotlights.spot_it: Squat grey concrete pillboxes with gun slits, half hidden in vegetation along the shore and on hilltops around the capital.
spotlights.story_md: Japan took the islands on **23 March 1942** without a fight; the British garrison was disarmed. The occupation that followed was one of the darkest periods in their history. Suspected spies were tortured in the Cellular Jail, the respected doctor **Diwan Singh** died of his injuries, and on **30 January 1944**, 44 civilians were shot at **Homfreyganj**. As food ran out in 1945, hundreds of people were shipped to an uninhabited island and left; only about a dozen were found alive. Roughly **2,000** people died, about a tenth of Port Blair's pre-war population. The bunkers are what remains.
spotlights.why_it_matters: They mark the only Indian territory occupied by Japan in the Second World War.
spotlights.memory_hook: Concrete pillboxes, the souvenirs of the islands' worst years.

spotlights.name: Bose raises the tricolour
spotlights.spot_it: A statue of Subhas Chandra Bose in uniform in the capital, and the stadium where he raised the flag.
spotlights.story_md: On **29 December 1943** Japan formally handed the islands to Subhas Chandra Bose's **Azad Hind** provisional government, and Bose flew in. On 30 December he raised the Indian tricolour at the Gymkhana ground in Port Blair, the first time it was flown on Indian soil freed from British rule. He renamed the islands **Shaheed** (Andaman) and **Swaraj** (Nicobar). The reality was grimmer: the Japanese kept control of the police, and the torture went on under the new flag. Exactly 75 years later, on 30 December 2018, the Prime Minister hoisted the flag at the same spot.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is the founding myth of the islands' place in the freedom struggle, with a complicated truth.
spotlights.memory_hook: Free India's first flag flew where Japan still held the keys.

spotlights.name: The renamed islands
spotlights.spot_it: Ferry tickets that now read Swaraj Dweep and Shaheed Dweep while everyone still says Havelock and Neil.
spotlights.story_md: Since 2018 the government has been rewriting the map. On **30 December 2018**, Ross Island became Netaji Subhas Chandra Bose Dweep, Neil became **Shaheed Dweep** and Havelock became **Swaraj Dweep**, using Bose's 1943 names. Havelock had been named after a British general who fought against the 1857 uprising. On **23 January 2023**, Bose's birthday, the **21 largest unnamed islands** were named after the 21 Param Vir Chakra winners; the largest honours Major Somnath Sharma. In 2021 Mount Harriet became Mount Manipur, and in **September 2024** Port Blair became Sri Vijaya Puram.
spotlights.why_it_matters: The names are now a statement about which history the islands should remember.
spotlights.memory_hook: 21 islands, 21 bravest soldiers.

sections.title: Who lives here now
sections.intro_md: Over 90% of today's islanders descend from people who arrived after 1858. Convicts came first, then Burmese Karen, Chotanagpur tribal workers and Moplah families from Malabar under the British. After 1947 the government settled refugees from East Pakistan and families from Tamil Nadu, Andhra, Kerala and elsewhere, partly to firm up India's claim to the islands. The result is a cross-section of India in miniature: Hindu about 69%, Christian 21%, Muslim 9% (2011), with Bengali the most spoken language and Hindi the shared one.

spotlights.name: Local borns and a mini India
spotlights.spot_it: A market where shop signs are in Bengali, Tamil and Hindi, people switch between them mid-sentence, and Hindi is the common tongue.
spotlights.story_md: Almost everyone in the islands descends from someone who came from elsewhere. The oldest settler families are the **local borns**, descendants of convicts from all over British India who married, stayed and lost their caste and region in the process. After 1947 came waves of settlers: refugees from East Bengal in the 1950s and 60s, Tamils, Telugus and Malayalis, ex-servicemen, and tribal workers from Chotanagpur, still called Ranchiwalas. The 2011 census shows the result: **Bengali 28%, Tamil 15%, Telugu 13%, Hindi 13%, Nicobarese 8%, Malayalam 7%**. Hindi is the bridge language, with an accent of its own.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is one of the few places in India where caste and region were partly erased by history.
spotlights.memory_hook: A society built by convicts, refugees and settlers.

spotlights.name: The Karen of Webi
spotlights.spot_it: Villages near Mayabunder where people speak S'gaw Karen, sing Baptist hymns and fish from dugouts like their Burmese ancestors.
spotlights.story_md: In **1925**, thirteen Karen families from Burma arrived in the Andamans, brought by the colonial forest department to work the timber and encouraged by Baptist missionaries. About 50 more families followed in 1926. They founded the village of **Webi** on Middle Andaman, the first Karen village in India. By 2004 there were about **2,000 Karen** in eight villages around Mayabunder and Diglipur. They still speak S'gaw Karen, are mostly Christian, and are known as the best boatmen and woodsmen in the north. Most mainland Indians have never heard that there is an Indian Karen community.
spotlights.why_it_matters: They are the islands' least known settler people, a piece of Myanmar inside India.
spotlights.memory_hook: A Burmese village in India since 1925.

sections.title: Nicobarese art, houses, food
sections.intro_md: The settler towns cook and celebrate like the mainland regions they came from: Durga Puja in Bengali neighbourhoods, Pongal in Tamil ones, Onam in Malayali ones. The distinctive island culture belongs to the Nicobarese. Their carved spirit figures, beehive houses, outrigger canoes and pandanus food grew out of life on small coral islands, and much of it was shaken by the 2004 tsunami and the rebuilding that followed. Food across the islands is about the sea and the coconut.

spotlights.name: Kareau, the Nicobarese spirit scarer
spotlights.spot_it: A carved, painted wooden figure, often a man in a top hat or with raised arms, set in a house to frighten off harmful spirits.
spotlights.story_md: Nicobarese households traditionally kept carved and painted wooden figures called **kareau** (also known as hentakoi) to keep away disease-bringing spirits. Shamans guided their making and use. What surprises museum visitors is the costume: many kareau wear European **top hats** and coats, the dress of the traders and colonial officials who arrived by ship, sometimes with wings or animal heads. The figure borrowed the look of powerful outsiders to scare off other powerful outsiders. Museums in London and Kolkata hold examples; in the islands, Christianity has made new ones rare.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is the islands' most original art form.
spotlights.memory_hook: A ghost-scarer in a sea captain's top hat.

spotlights.name: The Nicobari beehive hut
spotlights.spot_it: A round, dome-shaped thatched house raised on tall posts, entered through a trapdoor by a ladder.
spotlights.story_md: The traditional Nicobari house is a **dome of thatch on stilts**, as much as 2 m off the ground. The height kept out damp, pigs, snakes and floods, and the space underneath was used for work, canoes and livestock. You climb in through a hole in the floor and pull the ladder up behind you. Several families might share one large house, and villages often had separate birth houses and death houses. After the 2004 tsunami, the government rebuilt thousands of homes in concrete and tin, and true beehive huts are now rare outside museums and ceremonies.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is architecture fitted exactly to a hot, wet, low island.
spotlights.memory_hook: Pull the ladder up and the house is locked.

spotlights.name: Nicobarese canoes and canoe racing
spotlights.spot_it: A long, narrow outrigger canoe with a single float, raced by teams of paddlers in a fierce sprint.
spotlights.story_md: Canoes are the Nicobarese's road, net and pride. A traditional canoe is carved from a single trunk and balanced by one outrigger float. Long racing canoes, paddled by big crews, compete at village festivals, and the races are both sport and a show of community strength. Canoe racing also features at the islands' Tourism Festival, now held each year. Pigs and coconuts are the other measures of wealth, and the biggest event of the Nicobarese year was once the **Ossuary feast**, when the bones of the dead were dug up, cleaned and honoured with pig sacrifices and dancing.
spotlights.why_it_matters: The canoe made it possible to live on scattered small islands.
spotlights.memory_hook: One tree, one float, one village racing.

spotlights.name: Pandanus, the Nicobar staple
spotlights.spot_it: A huge, heavy fruit like a pineapple made of orange wedges, boiled into a paste that keeps for weeks.
spotlights.story_md: Long before rice arrived, the Nicobarese and Shompen lived on **pandanus**, the screw pine. Its big compound fruit is made of hard wedges that are boiled, scraped and pressed into a thick paste, which can be eaten fresh or stored. Together with coconut, pigs, fish and tubers it made up a complete island diet. The coconut was so central that for centuries it was the main thing islanders traded with passing ships. Today rice, dal and fish curry dominate, but pandanus paste and smoked pork still mark Nicobarese feasts.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is the food that made the Nicobars liveable without farms.
spotlights.memory_hook: A fruit you have to boil and scrape before you can eat it.

spotlights.name: Fish curry and the settler table

where.label: Mohanpura fish market, Sri Vijaya Puram

spotlights.spot_it: Marlin, tuna, reef fish and prawns on market slabs; at home, a red coconut fish curry or Bengali macher jhol with rice.
spotlights.story_md: There is no single Andaman cuisine because the islands were peopled from everywhere. A Bengali family cooks **macher jhol**, a Tamil family a tamarind fish kuzhambu, a Malayali family a coconut curry, all with the same fish from the same market. What unites them is the sea: grilled lobster and crab for tourists, tuna, marlin and reef fish for everyone else, and coconut in almost everything. The fisheries potential is large; the islands give India nearly a third of its Exclusive Economic Zone, yet much of the deep-sea catch is still taken by foreign poachers.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Food here is a map of where the settlers came from.
spotlights.memory_hook: Five cuisines, one fish market.

spotlights.name: Coconut, the island economy
spotlights.spot_it: Dense groves of coconut palms, split nuts drying in the sun as copra, and thatch, rope and mats everywhere.
spotlights.story_md: Coconut is the islands' oldest cash crop. The Nicobarese traded coconuts with passing ships for centuries; Danish and British traders came for copra, the dried kernel pressed for oil. Coconut palms cover most of the farmed land in the Nicobars, and the Andamans grow coconut, areca nut and spices on the small share of land that can be farmed, about **6%** of the territory. Prisoners in the Cellular Jail were made to turn oil mills to squeeze coconut oil to a daily quota, which makes the same nut a symbol of both island life and punishment.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It ties tribal trade, colonial plantations and jail labour into one story.
spotlights.memory_hook: The palm that paid the bills and punished prisoners.

sections.title: Where to go
sections.intro_md: Most visitors fly into Sri Vijaya Puram, do the Cellular Jail and the harbour islands, then take a ferry to Swaraj Dweep (Havelock) and Shaheed Dweep (Neil). The best season is November to April; the south-west monsoon from May to September brings rough seas and cancelled ferries. The Nicobars are mostly closed to tourists and need special permits, and tribal reserves are off limits. Indian visitors need no permit for the main tourist islands; foreign visitors may need one depending on where they go. The quieter north, Diglipur and Saddle Peak, is a long road or ferry trip away.

spotlights.name: Radhanagar Beach
spotlights.spot_it: A 2 km curve of powder-white sand backed by tall forest, with calm turquoise water and a famous sunset.
spotlights.story_md: Radhanagar, Beach No. 7 on Swaraj Dweep (Havelock), became famous when **Time magazine** featured it in **2004** among the world's best beaches, and it has since earned **Blue Flag** certification for clean water and management. What makes it different from many Asian beaches is the backdrop: a wall of tall tropical forest right behind the sand, not hotels. It is about **2 km** long. The sunset draws crowds every evening, and lifeguards patrol because the gentle-looking surf can hide currents. Go at dawn and you may have it nearly to yourself.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is the single image most people have of the Andamans.
spotlights.memory_hook: Beach Number 7, the one Time put on the world map.

spotlights.name: The natural bridge, Shaheed Dweep
spotlights.spot_it: A rock arch of old coral standing over a shore of tide pools, reachable only when the tide is out.
spotlights.story_md: Neil Island is small enough to cycle around in a day, and its best-known sight is a **natural rock arch** formed from ancient coral and limestone that the sea has carved through. It is often called the Howrah Bridge by visitors. You can only walk out to it at low tide, across sharp dead coral full of pools where sea cucumbers, starfish and small fish are stranded until the water returns. The 2004 earthquake raised parts of the coast here, which is one reason so much old reef is now exposed. Wear shoes: the coral is hard on feet.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It shows the islands' raised coral geology in one frame.
spotlights.memory_hook: A bridge made of reef that the sea forgot.

spotlights.name: Ross and Smith islands

where.label: Off Aerial Bay, Diglipur, North Andaman

spotlights.spot_it: Two forested islands joined by a narrow curving spit of white sand, with the sea on both sides.
spotlights.story_md: In the far north near Diglipur, two small islands are joined by a **sandbar** you can walk along, with water lapping on both sides. At high tide it narrows, and at times the sea nearly covers it. The area is also the gateway to **Saddle Peak**, at **732 m** the highest point in the islands, and to beaches where turtles nest. Few visitors make the 300 km trip north on the Andaman Trunk Road, so Diglipur gives a sense of what Havelock felt like before tourism. A permit is needed because the islands are a wildlife sanctuary.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It shows the quieter north that most tourists never reach.
spotlights.memory_hook: Two islands holding hands across a strip of sand.

spotlights.name: North Bay and its lighthouse

where.label: North Bay Island, opposite Sri Vijaya Puram

spotlights.when: Lighthouse on the old 20 rupee note
spotlights.spot_it: A red and white lighthouse above coconut palms and a coral beach, seen from the capital across the bay.
spotlights.story_md: North Bay is the easiest coral reef to reach from the capital, a short boat ride across the harbour, with glass-bottom boats, snorkelling and sea walks. Its red and white lighthouse is the one visible in the view from Mount Harriet that went onto the old **20 rupee note**. Together with Ross Island and Viper Island it makes up the standard harbour tour, which takes in a colonial ruin, a gallows and a reef in one morning. For snorkellers who want more, Elephant Beach on Swaraj Dweep and Jolly Buoy in the marine park are the next steps.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is where most visitors see coral for the first time.
spotlights.memory_hook: The lighthouse from the money.

sections.title: The morning of 26 December 2004
sections.intro_md: The Sumatra-Andaman earthquake was one of the largest ever recorded, and the islands sat right on top of the rupture. There was almost no warning time: the first waves arrived within minutes. The Nicobars, low and flat, suffered most; the Air Force base on Car Nicobar was destroyed, and whole villages on Katchal and Great Nicobar vanished. The land itself moved. Some places sank and stayed under water, others rose and left reefs dry. The disaster also produced the islands' most famous survival story, the Onge's.

spotlights.name: 26 December 2004
spotlights.spot_it: The water drew back from beaches, then came in three or four waves; on Car Nicobar the third wave was about 11 m.
spotlights.story_md: The **magnitude 9.1 to 9.3** earthquake off Sumatra ruptured the seafloor for about **1,300 to 1,600 km**, right up under the islands. The waves reached them within minutes, not hours. Port Blair, sheltered by hills, saw waves of about 3 m. Car Nicobar's flat east coast took waves of about **11 m** that wrecked the Indian Air Force base and carried oil tankers 800 m inland. On Little Andaman the fourth wave, about 10 m, flattened Hut Bay. Thousands died across the territory; counts of dead and missing range from about 3,500 to more than 6,000.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It reshaped the land, the coast and the society of the islands in one morning.
spotlights.memory_hook: The wave came in minutes, not hours.

spotlights.name: Indira Point
spotlights.spot_it: A lighthouse among palms at the very southern tip of Great Nicobar, with the sea now lapping much closer than it used to.
spotlights.story_md: India's southernmost point is not Kanyakumari. It is **Indira Point** on Great Nicobar, at about 6.75 degrees north. In 2004 the earthquake dropped the ground here by **4.25 m**, the sea flooded the point, and the base of its 35 m lighthouse was left standing in water. The land around it is gone. Elsewhere the movement went the other way: parts of the north and North Sentinel rose by about 1.5 m, lifting reefs into the air. In one morning the country's southern edge moved inland and its map changed for good.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is the place where the 2004 quake literally moved India's border with the sea.
spotlights.memory_hook: India's last point sank four metres in a morning.

spotlights.name: Katchal
spotlights.spot_it: A low, palm-covered island in the central Nicobars, quiet now, where the worst of 2004 happened.
spotlights.story_md: No island suffered more in 2004. Of Katchal's roughly **5,300** people, about **300 to 350 were confirmed dead**, and counts of the missing run from about **1,500 to 4,350**; most were never found. The island is flat and its villages lay right behind the beaches. Before the tsunami, Katchal had been famous for something else: travellers had converged on it to watch the first sunrise of the year 2000, because it lies so far east and south. Five years later its coastal villages were gone. Survivors were rehoused, and many Nicobarese communities moved away from the shore for good.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is the human scale of the disaster in one island.
spotlights.memory_hook: First to see the millennium sunrise, worst hit five years later.

sections.title: Strategy, timber and tourists
sections.intro_md: The islands' economy is small, about ₹12,500 crore in 2023-24, with per-head income around ₹3.1 lakh, above the national average largely because of government salaries. Timber was king until felling was restricted in 2002. Tourism is now the engine, along with fisheries, coconut and areca. Connectivity was a weakness until August 2020, when a 2,312 km undersea fibre cable from Chennai brought fast internet to seven islands. But the islands' real value to India is strategic: they sit astride the western approach to the Strait of Malacca.

spotlights.name: Andaman and Nicobar Command
spotlights.spot_it: Grey warships in Port Blair harbour, runways at Car Nicobar and Campbell Bay, and joint exercises with foreign navies.
spotlights.story_md: The islands are India's front door on the **Strait of Malacca**, through which a large share of the world's sea trade and much of China's oil passes. In **2001** India set up the **Andaman and Nicobar Command**, its first and still only joint command where army, navy, air force and coast guard serve under one chief. It runs air stations at Car Nicobar, Shibpur in the north (INS Kohassa) and Campbell Bay (INS Baaz, India's southernmost air station). The command hosts the MILAN exercise, where navies from across the Indian Ocean meet at Port Blair.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It turns the islands from a remote outpost into India's main lookout over the Malacca Strait.
spotlights.memory_hook: India's only tri-service command watches the world's busiest strait.

spotlights.name: Chatham Saw Mill
spotlights.spot_it: Long tin-roofed sheds on a small island joined to the capital by a bridge, smelling of fresh-cut timber.
spotlights.story_md: Chatham is where Archibald Blair set up the first British post in 1789, and where the colonial timber industry was born. The **saw mill**, founded in **1883**, cut padauk, gurjan and other hardwoods for buildings in India and Britain, and it is often described as one of the oldest and largest in Asia. Japanese bombs hit it in the Second World War; the craters are still there. It still runs as a government enterprise, with 342 staff in 2024, and has a forest museum. Its slow decline tracks the island economy's shift from timber to tourism.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is the old economy you can still walk through.
spotlights.memory_hook: The island where Blair landed still saws wood.

spotlights.name: Veer Savarkar International Airport
spotlights.spot_it: A large new glass and steel terminal beside a single runway shared with the navy.
spotlights.story_md: Almost every visitor arrives by air, through one runway in the capital that also serves as a naval air station, **INS Utkrosh**. A new integrated terminal opened on **18 July 2023**: about **40,800 square metres** against the old building's 6,100, built for 1,200 passengers an hour. In 2025-26 the airport handled about **18 lakh** passengers. It is named after Savarkar. In 2024 the islands received about **7.1 lakh domestic and 11,500 foreign tourists**, more than double the number of people who live there, and nearly all came through this building or the ships at Haddo.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is the bottleneck through which the tourism boom flows.
spotlights.memory_hook: One runway, shared by fighters and families.

sections.title: What is happening now
sections.intro_md: Late 2026 finds the islands at a decision point. The Great Nicobar project has cleared the National Green Tribunal (16 February 2026), but the Calcutta High Court is due to hear the main challenge on 25 and 26 November 2026, after the Supreme Court in October 2026 declined to step in. Barren Island erupted repeatedly through late 2025 and into January 2026. The Baratang mud volcano blew on 2 October 2025. An American who landed on North Sentinel in March 2025 was arrested within days. And tourist numbers keep climbing, with officials calling 2025 a record year.

spotlights.name: The Great Nicobar project

where.label: Galathea Bay and Campbell Bay, Great Nicobar

spotlights.spot_it: Rainforest running down to a quiet bay on Great Nicobar, where a container port, airport, power plant and city are planned.
spotlights.story_md: Proposed by NITI Aayog in 2021, the **Great Nicobar project** would build an international container trans-shipment port at **Galathea Bay**, a dual-use airport, a gas and solar power plant and a township, at a cost now put at about **₹81,000 crore**. Over **130 square km** of the 166 square km site is forest, and roughly a million trees would be cut. Supporters say it gives India a port on the Malacca route to rival Singapore and Colombo. Critics point to the leatherback nesting beach, earthquake risk, and the Shompen. In February 2026 the National Green Tribunal upheld the clearances; the Calcutta High Court hears the main challenge in November 2026.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is the biggest decision about the islands' future since independence.
spotlights.memory_hook: A Singapore-sized bet on a turtle beach.

best_facts.fact: India's southernmost point is not Kanyakumari but Indira Point on Great Nicobar, and in 2004 the earthquake dropped it 4.25 m into the sea.
best_facts.why_surprising: Most Indians learn the wrong answer at school, and the right one sank.

best_facts.fact: The Onge of Little Andaman survived the 2004 tsunami almost to a person because an old story told them that a big shaking is followed by a wall of water.
best_facts.why_surprising: Oral tradition beat modern warning systems.

best_facts.fact: Three days after the 2004 earthquake, Sentinelese on the beach shot arrows and threw spears and stones at a government helicopter sent to check on them.
best_facts.why_surprising: Survival first, then a very clear message: leave us alone.

best_facts.fact: Lord Mayo is the only Viceroy of India ever assassinated, stabbed by a convict at a Port Blair jetty in 1872.
best_facts.why_surprising: The most powerful man in India died in its remotest prison colony.

best_facts.fact: Boa Sr, the last speaker of Bo, spent decades with no one left who understood her language. When she died in 2010, the language died too.
best_facts.why_surprising: A language possibly tens of thousands of years old ended with one woman.

best_facts.fact: The Great Andamanese fell from thousands of people to just 19 in 1961, mostly through diseases brought by colonial contact.
best_facts.why_surprising: Ten tribes nearly vanished within a century.

best_facts.fact: The Nicobar Islands were a Danish colony for about a century and were sold to Britain only in 1868.
best_facts.why_surprising: Part of India was once Danish.

best_facts.fact: The name Nicobar probably comes from Ma-Nakkavaram, a word in a Chola inscription at Thanjavur from about 1050 CE.
best_facts.why_surprising: A Tamil temple wall named a whole island group.

best_facts.fact: Barren Island, India's only active volcano, is home to no people, only feral goats descended from animals left by sailors in 1891.
best_facts.why_surprising: A live volcano with goats as its only residents.

best_facts.fact: The Cellular Jail's wings were arranged so that every cell door faced the blank back wall of the next wing.
best_facts.why_surprising: Isolation was built into the architecture.

best_facts.fact: The Nicobar pigeon's closest living relative was the dodo.
best_facts.why_surprising: A shiny island pigeon is the dodo's nearest surviving cousin.

best_facts.fact: The Nicobar megapode does not sit on its eggs; it buries them in compost mounds up to 10 cubic metres, and the chicks can fly as soon as their feathers dry.
The view on the back of the old 20 rupee note is from Mount Harriet, above Port Blair.
best_facts.why_surprising: Millions carried an Andaman postcard in their wallets.

best_facts.fact: Bengali, not Hindi, is the most spoken language in the islands, at about 28% in 2011.
best_facts.why_surprising: A Bay of Bengal territory speaks the Bay's language.

best_facts.fact: Timber elephants in the Andamans had to learn to swim in the open sea to tow logs to barges; the last famous one, Rajan, became a diving celebrity.
best_facts.why_surprising: Elephants are not native, yet one became a sea swimmer.

best_facts.fact: In March 2025 an American YouTuber landed on North Sentinel and left a can of Diet Coke and a coconut as an offering; he was arrested within days.
best_facts.why_surprising: A soft drink can on the world's most isolated beach.

best_facts.fact: The Baratang mud volcano's October 2025 eruption threw up material dated to about 23 million years ago.
best_facts.why_surprising: A volcano that spits out ancient seafloor, cold.

best_facts.fact: In 2024 the islands received about 7.1 lakh domestic tourists, nearly twice their 2011 population.

side_dish.title: What the Andamanese genome tells us
side_dish.body_md: When geneticists started reading the DNA of the Onge, Jarawa and Great Andamanese, many expected a time capsule: a people isolated so long that they might preserve a separate, earlier migration out of Africa. The answer was more interesting. All Onge men carry a Y-chromosome lineage called haplogroup D, which is rare in mainland India. A 2017 study of Indian Y chromosomes concluded that this does not mean a separate ancestry: haplogroup D was part of the ordinary variation carried by the same out-of-Africa expansion that peopled all of Asia, and it was later lost in most other populations. The Jarawa and Onge seem to have shared their lineage within the last 7,000 years or so, a sign that their numbers were small for a long time. Geneticists now use the Andamanese as an imperfect stand-in for a very old strand of ancestry, often called Ancient Ancestral South Indian, which forms part of the genes of most people in India today. Their short stature and dark skin, once used to lump them with African pygmies, do not reflect close African kinship: studies show the so-called Negrito groups of Asia do not share a common origin apart from other Asians, so the resemblance is likely convergence, bodies shaped by similar rainforest lives. The lesson matches the tsunami story: small, isolated peoples carry knowledge, in their stories and in their genes, that the rest of us have lost.

offline_task.title: Find the Andamans in your wallet and on your map
offline_task.body_md: If you have an old 20 rupee note from before 2019, turn it over: the palms and sea are the view from Mount Harriet, now Mount Manipur, above Port Blair. If you do not, open any printed map of India and find the islands, usually tucked in a box in the corner. Now check where they really are: draw a line from Indira Point to Sumatra and another to Chennai, and compare. Then name three things on the islands you could see without a permit (Cellular Jail, Radhanagar, Ross Island) and two places nobody may visit (North Sentinel, the Jarawa reserve). Five minutes, and the corner box will never look like an afterthought again.
